Bizarre

/biz-AR/ — stress on second syllable, rhymes with far · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something bizarre is so odd or out of the ordinary that it seems strange or hard to believe.

The garden was full of bizarre sculptures, including a giant fork stuck in the lawn.

Worked Example

The garden was full of bizarre sculptures, including a giant fork stuck in the lawn, rubber ducks painted neon pink, and a chandelier hanging from a tree branch.

Bizarre is more precise than 'strange' because it captures extreme and shocking oddness—so unusual it's hard to believe. 'Strange' just means surprising; bizarre means strangely extreme to the point of being unbelievable.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

outlandish: Outlandish means wildly odd, as if from another world — outfits, schemes, and claims can all be outlandish. It overlaps with bizarre at the extreme end, but outlandish carries a note of showy absurdity, while bizarre stresses oddness so extreme it is genuinely hard to believe.

peculiar: Peculiar means noticeably odd in a distinctive way — a peculiar smell, a peculiar habit — and it stays mild, more puzzling than shocking. Bizarre sits far beyond it: something bizarre is so extremely odd that people struggle to believe or even classify it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ordinary: completely usual, with nothing surprising about it

unremarkable: so normal it draws no attention

Where it sits · how strikingly odd it is — ordinary → strange → weird → bizarre

ordinary vs. bizarre: Ordinary is the opposite end of the scale from bizarre: an ordinary sight blends in completely, while a bizarre one stops you in your tracks.

strange vs. bizarre: Strange is weaker than bizarre; a strange sight makes you look twice, but a bizarre one is so wildly odd it is hard to believe.

weird vs. bizarre: Weird is stronger than strange, but bizarre tops them both: weird things feel off or eerie, while bizarre things are outlandishly, almost absurdly odd.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — bizarre

Root — bizarre: odd, eccentric (earlier 'quick-tempered') (Italian (via French))

Put it together

Put it together: Bizarre cannot be broken into smaller English pieces: it was borrowed whole from Italian bizzarro, whose meaning drifted from 'quick-tempered' to 'eccentric' to 'strange' — giving English a word for anything so odd it is hard to believe.

Use the root in a new word: bizarrely

Use the root in a new word: bizarrely: The house was bizarrely decorated, with upside-down furniture glued to the ceiling — bizarrely is simply bizarre plus -ly, describing how strangely something is done.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Use bizarre when describing things so shockingly odd they're hard to believe or classify. For mild strangeness or everyday surprises, 'strange' or 'weird' are simpler and often better.
